sections.html:
• Scientific name: Noturus gladiator Thomas & Burr, 2004
  • Common name: Piebald Madtom
  • Size: 107 mm (4.2") SL
  • IUCN Red List: Near Threatened (last assessed 2012)

North America: coastal plain streams of Tennessee and Mississippi, USA. Gulf Coast drainages, Mississippi. Type locality: just upstream of Potters Creek, about 2.5 km west of Bolivar, Pleasant Run, Hatchie River at Summerville-Bolivar Road, Mississippi River basin, Hardeman County, Tennessee, U.S.A.

North America: Coastal plain streams of Tennessee and Mississippi, USA. Type locality: Tennessee: Hardeman County: Mississippi River basin, Pleasant Run (Hatchie River) at Summerville-Bolivar Rd., just upstream of Potters Creek, ca. 2.5 km W of Bolivar; 35º15'14"N, 089º02'05"W.

Inhabits mainstream rivers of small to medium size and the lower reaches of their major tributaries. Most commonly associated with moderate velocities, moderate depth (about 60 cm), clean sand or clay substrata and cover in the form of leaf packs, brush and log jams.

The madtoms are well suited to aquarium life. Provide river gravel and smooth rounded stones for hiding places during the day. A power filter at one end of the tank will provide the conditions of a flowing stream for these catfish.
They like most meaty food, such as cut-up earth worms, frozen blood worm and prawns. They will also take tablet and pellet foods. A varied diet will keep them in optimum health.
Can be housed with other North American fishes such as minnows, darters and shiners.
Breeding: unreported. There is no breeding report.

Etymology: from the Greek notos, meaning back, and oura, meaning tail, in reference to the confluent adipose and caudal fins. The specific epithet refers to the large, serrated pectoral spines (gladiator = swordsman).

Description: Dorsal spines (total): 1; dorsal soft rays (total): 6-7; anal soft rays: 12-15; vertebrae: 33-34. Differs also by the following combination of characters: pectoral spine with strongly developed anterior dentations, some often bifurcate; pectoral spine, its posterior serrae, and the posterior process of cleithrum very large; pectoral fin long, sickle-shaped, and when depressed, reaching beyond pelvic fin origin, except in very large specimens. A member of the Noturus furiosus species group and formerly part of the N. stigmosus complex.

Colouration: Distinguished from all other members by its exceptionally bold pigment pattern: dark brown to black dorsal saddles highly contrasted with pale yellow to tan areas on the body; the posterior dark saddle passing through the adipose fin extends to the middle of the anal fin base, posterior to the terminus of the caudal peduncle, forming a well-defined broad lateral band of dense pigment; dorsal fin with dark, broad submarginal and basal bands connected anteriorly via the first 2-3 rays; anal fin with a dark central blotch extending onto the base and often connected to intense dark pigment on the sides of the caudal peduncle; dark, crescent-shaped midcaudal band, thickest in the center where broadly joined to dark pigment on the caudal peduncle.

Etymology: The specific name gladiator is from the Latin gladiator, meaning swordsman, in reference to the large and serrated pectoral spines of this species (Noturus).

Remarks: Previously known under the name Noturus stigmosus or N. sp. cf. stigmosus.

IUCN Red List: This species is listed as Near Threatened because its area of occupancy may be less than 2,000 sq km and distribution, abundance, and habitat quantity and quality are subject to ongoing declines. However, the estimated number of locations exceeds 10, the distribution is not severely fragmented, and the rate of decline is probably not more than 30 percent over 10 years or three generations, therefore the species does not fully qualify for Vulnerable status.
Ichthyological Exploration of Freshwaters v. 15 (no. 4), pp 353, Figs. 2-3, 8c.
